summary: Academic mining study (Melbourne, SMU, Heidelberg) of how agent skills (SKILL.md) move from a central registry into repositories and are maintained there. It collects 18,463 skills.sh registry skills (>=20 installs, 4 Mar 2026) and 23,199 personal-use skills in 5,876 GitHub repos (>=10 stars, aggregators filtered), links 3,709 repo skills to registry origins (YAML name plus LCS similarity, audited), classifies software-engineering knowledge areas with Qwen3.6-27B (kappa 0.82 vs 285 gold labels), thematically codes 180 skill bodies, and codes 444 endpoint diffs (188 linked, 256 unlinked) for evolution and customisation edits.

claims.claim: Skills are mostly copied once and not maintained: most linked copies are near-verbatim and never updated locally, and many miss upstream updates.
claims.evidence: 1,841/2,462 SE links near-verbatim; 70.3% of all links have similarity >= 0.99; 1,295 (52.6%) never locally updated; 40.2% of those missed upstream changes; 62.3% (429/689) of updated copies diverged from the registry. Link audit: 30+30 pairs, 90% agreement, 93% genuine.

claims.claim: Maintenance is additive: edits accrete content far more than they remove it.
claims.evidence: Additions:removals 586:221 (2.7:1) overall; 6.1:1 for evolution vs 1.1:1 for customisation. Based on 444 first-vs-last endpoint diffs, so intermediate churn is invisible; content-type coding of diffs has no reported agreement.

claims.claim: Customisation primarily adapts skills to local environments, while evolution accumulates domain knowledge.
claims.evidence: Table III (Fisher with BH): repackaging 12.2% vs 0% (h=0.71), reformatting 48.9% vs 20.4%, revising inline knowledge 19.7% vs 32.5%, renames 5.3% vs 24.3%. The most frequent customisation edit is reformatting, not environment adaptation, so the 'local environment' framing is partly an interpretation.

claims.claim: The behavioural contract (user interaction, monitoring, failure handling) is rarely edited.
claims.evidence: User-interaction content edited in 1.6%/1.2% of diffs, monitoring 0.5%/0.0%, failure handling 5.9%/7.1%. Absence of edits is not shown to be absence of need; no reliability statistic for the content-type labels.

claims.claim: Software Construction dominates SE skills in both registry and repositories.
claims.evidence: 28.3% registry, 22.1% repositories; LLM classifier validated at kappa 0.82 on 285 stratified gold labels.

patterns.note: Descriptive data on how on-demand SKILL.md skills are distributed, copied and edited; no outcome comparison of skills vs no skills.

85% of coded skill bodies 'ground domain knowledge', so skills are a de facto channel for machine-readable domain context; the paper shows this knowledge goes stale and accretes, but does not measure effect on agent behaviour.
Skills co-located with repo instruction files; conformance to the SKILL.md spec is high (mandatory fields >= 99%, name format 95-96%).
Some skills encode consent gating ('ask before ...'), but such behavioural-contract content is almost never edited; no evaluation.
63% of coded skills include interacting-with-the-user content and 22% gathering input, including front-door alignment/clarification skills; descriptive only, no comparison.

methodology.sample: 18,463 registry skills (skills.sh, >=20 installs) and 23,199 repository skills in 5,876 public GitHub repos (>=10 stars, aggregator filters, Tukey cap of 18 skills per repo); 3,709 registry-to-repo links; 180 coded bodies; 444 coded diffs.
methodology.baselines: Linked (registry-derived) vs unlinked (locally authored) skills; registry vs repository distributions. No outcome baseline.
methodology.models: Qwen3.6-27B for knowledge-area classification only; no agent runs.
methodology.variance: Fisher exact tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction and effect sizes for edit categories; classifier kappa 0.82; link audit agreement 90%.
methodology.ablations: Link similarity threshold sensitivity discussed; no other ablations (not applicable to a mining study).
methodology.languages: Natural-language SKILL.md files across public GitHub repos of all languages; no per-language breakdown.

biases.detail: Only public repos with >=10 stars and registry skills with >=20 installs; 1,367 inaccessible skills dropped. Private enterprise repos, where domain-knowledge skills matter most, are absent.
Edits are coded from first-vs-last snapshots, hiding intermediate add-then-remove churn and possibly overstating the additive pattern.
Thematic coding of 180 bodies and content-type coding of 444 diffs report no inter-rater agreement, unlike the link audit and classifier.
No measurement of whether stale, diverged or accreted skills change agent behaviour or task success; maintenance 'problems' are inferred from text alone.

coi.affiliations: University of Melbourne, Singapore Management University, Heidelberg University (academic).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: skills.sh registry and SKILL.md ecosystem; no vendor affiliation found.

verdict_reason: Large, careful and replicable descriptive study; the copy-once/never-update finding is well supported by audited links. Caveats: public starred repos only, endpoint diffs, unreported agreement for the qualitative coding, the 'local environment' customisation framing over-reads a reformatting-dominated distribution, and no evidence about agent outcomes.
applicability: Directly relevant to capturing knowledge back: domain knowledge written into SKILL.md or AGENTS.md files is copied once and drifts silently, and edits mostly add content. For four or more ingestion repos with mixed agent hosts: keep healthcare-education domain knowledge (glossary, content-type rules, accreditation constraints) in one versioned source and reference it by pointer instead of copying it into each repo; record provenance and version in each consuming skill and fail CI when the upstream version has moved; schedule pruning reviews because accretion is the default; use an agent-neutral layout (e.g. .agents/skills) since repackaging between host formats was 12.2% of customisation edits. The study is descriptive, so it says nothing about whether better-maintained skills improve agent results.

conflicts_with.detail: That study reports 89.3% of 138,133 SKILL.md files violate the spec, whereas this one finds >=95-99% conformance on mandatory fields; the difference likely comes from population (starred repos vs all files) and which spec rules are counted.
